newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Union leader urges LDCs to ponder labour objections.
newsitem.headline: Union leader urges LDCs to ponder labour objections.

text.p: An international trade union leader urged developing nations on Tuesday to reconsider their fierce opposition to using the World Trade Organisation (WTO) as a forum for ending labour rights abuse.

Bill Jordan of the International Confederation of Free Trades Unions (ICFTU) said it was true some western nations were trying to put the issue on the WTO agenda as a means of eroding the developing world's commercial advantage of cheap labour.

But he told Reuters Television the real thrust of the campaign was to use the WTO court to help improve often appalling working conditions in developing nations and put an estimated 250 million child workers in school.
"We are for the other form of protectionism -- protecting people from abuse," said Jordan, the Secretary General of the ICFTU which claims 124 million affiliated members in 136 countries.
Later, Jordan told a news conference that a WTO accord on the linking of core labour standards to trade would mark significant progress on the world human rights agenda.

"The only issue that the WTO is ignoring is the labour issue and it's an issue that affects more people in the world than any other," Jordan said on the fringes of the first ministerial meeting of the 128-member WTO.
He said the ICFTU was not looking for the WTO to take over labour issues from the International Labour Organisation (ILO), but to provide much needed muscle to back up the ILO's work.
"We are trying to bring home to the WTO the reality of global trade and what it is doing to labour standards around the world," Jordan said.
"What we are seeing now is all forms of labour rights abuse showing a startling increase. The number of children working is continuing to rise," he said.
Led by the United States, several countries are trying to persuade members at the five-day conference, which opened on Monday, to put labour rights on the WTO agenda.
But all the signs are that Washington is fighting a losing battle, with some Asian nations apparently refusing to consider even mentioning the issue in the conference's final declaration.
They argue, with support from several European nations and Australia, that the method of making goods is no business of an organisation dedicated to regulating international trade.
They believe that behind fine western words on improving the lot of the poor, is a bid to use the WTO to impose penalties on goods produced by cheap labour in the developing world.
Malaysian Trade Minister Rafidah Aziz said earlier on Tuesday the Group of 15 (G15) developing nations believed labour standards should not be in the programme of the WTO.
However, Sweden's Minister for Trade, Bjorn von Sydow, told the conference that the WTO and world trade ministers should give their support to continued work in the ILO.

"I think everyone who has spoken on this issue has underlined that we reject taking trade restrictive measures as a means to enforce labour standards and that the comparative advantage of low-wage countries must not be questioned," he said.
Jordan said the ICFTU wanted the issue on the WTO agenda so that its trade disputes court could be used as a last resort.
The WTO should, as several Scandinavian countries have proposed, set up a committee to deal with the issue and investigate alleged abuses, he said.
"If it identifies a particular objectionable or unnecessary form of abuse in a particular country, it would ask it to institute a process of reform," he said.
"Then we would call on the developed world to put their money where their mouth is and help fund the eradication of the problem," he added.
